title: Layer Cake

coach.board: The cards are the Dockerfile, top line first. Before a build, a prediction panel asks which layers will rebuild; after it, the layer panel shows each layer, whether it came from cache, and the image size.
coach.actions: Build runs your Dockerfile, once you have answered the prediction. Builds are limited, and each wrong prediction costs a little build budget.
coach.firstMove: Move the cards into a sensible order (drag the grip, or use Up and Down), then tap the layers you expect to rebuild after a source edit, lock it in, and press Build.

lossRule: The build budget ran out before the image met the goal.

events.title: A teammate edited a source file
events.fix: COPY and ADD are cache-busted by the content of the files they copy, so that layer and every layer after it rebuild. Copy the dependency manifest and install first, and the slow install stays cached.

events.title: A teammate changed the dependency manifest
events.fix: A changed manifest legitimately re-runs the install. That is the point of copying it on its own first: the install reruns only when the manifest changes, not on every code edit.

events.title: The base image was updated upstream
events.fix: A new base layer changes the cache key of everything built on it, so every layer rebuilds. Pin base image tags so that only happens when you choose.

events.title: CI started on a fresh runner with an empty cache
events.fix: With no cache every layer rebuilds. Carry a cache between runs: --cache-from, or cache-from/cache-to in docker/build-push-action.

events.title: The build failed: the Dockerfile does not start with FROM
events.fix: Every Dockerfile begins with FROM; any other instruction before it has no build stage to run in.

events.title: The build failed: the base image tag does not exist
events.fix: The registry has no such tag. Read the first ERROR line of the build log: it names the image it could not resolve.

events.title: The build failed: an instruction ran before its inputs were there
events.fix: Each instruction only sees what earlier layers put in the image. Read the failing step in the log, then check what it needs (a copied file, an installed dependency) is placed above it.

events.title: The build failed: COPY --from names a stage that does not exist
events.fix: COPY --from=NAME needs an earlier FROM ... AS NAME. Name the build stage, and copy from it only after the final stage's FROM.

events.title: The image is bigger than it needs to be
events.fix: A single-stage image ships the compiler, dev dependencies and source it only needed to build. Build in one stage and copy just the artifact into a small runtime stage.

events.title: The image builds but the container would not start
events.fix: A successful build only means every instruction ran. The container still needs a CMD (or a base image that has one), the files it runs, and any USER it names to exist.

events.title: A secret (.env) was baked into the image
events.fix: COPY . . copies everything in the build context, including .env. List secrets, .git and local dependency folders in a .dockerignore so they never enter the context or the image.

events.title: The build context is huge
events.fix: Docker sends the whole context to the builder on every build, and COPY . . puts all of it in a layer. A .dockerignore keeps .git, node_modules and virtualenvs out.

events.title: Package-manager cache was left in the image
events.fix: Files deleted in a later layer still exist in the earlier one, so cleanup has to happen in the same RUN that created them (apt-get install ... && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*).

events.title: The container runs as root
events.fix: The base image's default user is often root. Create an unprivileged user and switch to it with USER before CMD.

events.title: The api cannot reach the database: it connects to localhost
events.fix: Inside a container, localhost is the container itself. Services in a Compose project reach each other by service name, so point the api at db:5432.

events.title: The api started before the database accepted connections
events.fix: depends_on only orders container start, not readiness. Give db a healthcheck and make the api wait with condition: service_healthy.

events.title: The api waits for a healthy database, but db has no healthcheck
events.fix: condition: service_healthy needs a healthcheck on the service it waits for. Add one (pg_isready for Postgres).

events.title: Compose rejected the project: the volume is not declared
events.fix: A named volume used by a service must also be declared in the top-level volumes: section.

events.title: The database lost its data after down and up
events.fix: Data written to a container's writable layer is gone when the container is removed. Keep database data in a named volume.

events.title: The database port is published to the host
events.fix: Container-to-container traffic never needs a published port. Publish only what something outside Docker needs (web), and keep db off the host.

events.title: The web service is not reachable from the host
events.fix: A service is only reachable from outside Docker when it publishes a port, for example ports: ["8080:80"].

events.title: The database data lives in a bind mount
events.fix: A bind mount survives down, but it ties the stack to one host path and is not portable or reproducible in CI. Use a named volume for data you want to keep.

levels.title: 1. Hello nginx
levels.blurb: Arrange the cards into the Dockerfile from topics/docker/examples/hello-nginx so it builds and serves the page. Before each build, predict which layers will rebuild: a teammate edits index.html, then the base image is updated upstream.
hints: Look at the card tray: each card is one line of the Dockerfile, and the order is the build order. Predict the rebuilds before each build: the base layer is cached unless the base image changed.
A base image comes first, then the file you serve is copied in, then the port and the health check.
Arrange from-nginx, copy-index, expose-80, healthcheck, then Build twice: the second build shows what the cache reused.
path: Arrange the Dockerfile: from-nginx → copy-index → expose-80 → healthcheck
lessons: Every Dockerfile instruction is a layer, and the order of the instructions is the order of the build.
Docker reuses a layer from cache only when its instruction and every layer before it are unchanged.

tryItForReal.commands:
cd topics/docker/examples/hello-nginx
docker build -t hello-nginx .
docker run --rm -p 8080:80 hello-nginx      # then: curl localhost:8080
# edit index.html and build again: the base layers say CACHED

levels.title: 2. Cache order
levels.blurb: This Dockerfile works but reinstalls every dependency whenever anyone touches the code. Reorder it (and add what is missing) so edits rebuild only what they must. Predict the rebuilds before each build. You have four builds.
hints: Look at which steps rebuild when only the code changes: everything after a changed file runs again, so predict that cut-off before you build.
Copying all the code before installing dependencies invalidates the install layer on every edit.
Copy only the manifest, run npm ci, then copy the rest; add the cache flag so a fresh CI runner can reuse layers.
path: Arrange the Dockerfile: from-node → workdir → copy-manifest → npm-ci → copy-all → build → cmd-node
lessons: Copy the dependency manifest and install before you copy the source, so a code edit does not reinstall everything.
A fresh CI runner has no layer cache: export and import it, or every build starts cold.

tryItForReal.commands:
# Dockerfile
FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# on a CI runner
docker buildx build --cache-from type=gha --cache-to type=gha,mode=max -t app .

errors./app/package.json:
npm error code ENOENT
npm error path /app/package.json
npm error enoent Could not read package.json

errors./app/src: error: could not resolve entry module "src/main.js"

levels.title: 3. Slow CI
levels.blurb: CI starts every job on a fresh runner with an empty cache, so a good layer order alone is not enough: the build also needs --cache-from to bring the cache back. Arrange the Dockerfile, add the cache flag, and predict which layers rebuild before each of the five builds.

errors./app/package.json:
npm error code ENOENT
npm error path /app/package.json
npm error enoent Could not read package.json

errors./app/src: error: could not resolve entry module "src/main.js"

hints: Look at the build seconds after a cold runner: every layer rebuilt, even the ones nothing changed.
A fresh runner has no layer cache. The build flag card (--cache-from) imports the cache from where the last run stored it; without it every CI build is a cold one.
Order the Dockerfile manifest first, install, then the source, and add the cache flag card, then predict and build.
lessons: A CI runner starts empty, so layer order helps only if the cache comes with the job: --cache-from imports it and --cache-to exports it.
Predict a build before you run it: a cold runner rebuilds everything unless the cache is imported.

tryItForReal.needs: Docker with BuildKit (buildx) and a CI system that can store a cache
tryItForReal.commands:
# Dockerfile: manifest, install, then source
FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# in CI: import the cache, run the build, export it for the next job
docker buildx build \
  --cache-from type=registry,ref=registry.example.com/app:buildcache \
  --cache-to type=registry,ref=registry.example.com/app:buildcache,mode=max \
  -t app .

path: Arrange the Dockerfile: from-node → workdir → copy-manifest → npm-ci → copy-all → build → cmd-node → cache-flag

levels.title: 4. Bloat
levels.blurb: The app is a static site, but this image ships Node, every dependency and the source. Split it into a build stage and a small runtime stage so the final image is under 80 MB.
hints: Look at the final image size and what it still contains.
A multi-stage build keeps Node, the dependencies and the source in the first stage only.
Build in a node stage, then start a second FROM nginx and copy just the dist folder into it.
path: Arrange the Dockerfile: from-node-build → workdir → copy-manifest → npm-ci → copy-all → build → from-nginx → copy-dist → expose-80
lessons: A multi-stage build keeps compilers, dependencies and source in a build stage and ships only the result.
Pick the runtime image for what it must run: a static site needs a web server, not Node.

tryItForReal.commands:
# Dockerfile
FROM node:20-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:alpine
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html

docker build -t site . && docker images site   # compare the size

errors./app/package.json:
npm error code ENOENT
npm error path /app/package.json
npm error enoent Could not read package.json

errors./app/src: error: could not resolve entry module "src/main.js"

goal.requireWhy: the built site must end up where nginx serves it

levels.title: 5. Hygiene
levels.blurb: A Python service that builds, but the image is huge, leaks a secret, and runs as root. Pick the right variant of each card (and add what's missing) until it is under 200 MB, holds no secrets, and runs as a non-root user.
hints: Look at the three problems in the goal: size, a leaked secret and running as root.
A .dockerignore keeps secrets out of the build context, a slim base and clean apt and pip steps keep it small, and USER drops root.
Pick the dockerignore, the slim Python base, the apt-good and pip-good variants, then add useradd and user-app.
path: Arrange the Dockerfile: dockerignore → from-py → workdir → apt-good → copy-req → pip-good → copy-all → useradd → user-app → cmd-py
lessons: A .dockerignore keeps secrets and junk out of the build context; a secret copied into a layer stays in the image.
Use a slim base, clean package caches in the same layer, and switch to a non-root USER before the container starts.

tryItForReal.commands:
# .dockerignore
.env
.git
__pycache__/

# Dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN useradd --create-home app
USER app
CMD ["python", "main.py"]

cards.text: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

errors./app/requirements.txt: ERROR: Could not open requirements file: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'requirements.txt'
ERROR: Could not open requirements file: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'requirements.txt'

levels.title: 6. Broken build
levels.blurb: This build fails. Read the log, find the offending step, fix it, and repeat: there is more than one problem. Each failed build costs budget, so predict which line fails before you rebuild. When it finally builds, a teammate edits the source: predict what rebuilds.
hints: Predict which line fails before you build, then read the failed build log from the bottom: it names the step that broke.
There is more than one problem: fix one and the next step fails.
Copy the manifest before npm ci, copy the sources before the build step, and end with the CMD.
path: Arrange the Dockerfile: from-node → workdir → copy-manifest → npm-ci → copy-all → build → cmd-node
lessons: Read a failed build from the bottom: the last step that ran is the one that failed.
Fix one problem at a time and rebuild, and check what each instruction needs to exist before it runs (a manifest before npm ci, the sources before the build).

tryItForReal.commands:
docker build -t app . 2>&1 | tail -20      # read from the bottom
docker build --progress=plain -t app .      # full output of every step
docker history app                          # what each layer added

errors./app/package.json:
npm error code ENOENT
npm error path /app/package.json
npm error enoent Could not read package.json

errors./app/src: error: could not resolve entry module "src/main.js"

levels.title: 7. Compose wiring
levels.blurb: A web, api and db stack that does not work yet. Pick one line for each slot of compose.yaml so api reaches db by name, waits for it, and the data survives a down and up, without publishing anything that only containers need.
hints: Look at the three services and what each slot of compose.yaml connects.
Containers reach each other by service name, not localhost; depends_on only waits with a healthcheck; data needs a named volume.
Point the api at the host db, make it depend on db being healthy with a pg healthcheck, use a named volume, and publish nothing on db.
lessons: Containers on one Compose network reach each other by service name, never localhost; publish a port only for what the host must reach.
depends_on only waits for a service to be healthy if it has a healthcheck, and data survives down and up only in a named volume.

tryItForReal.commands:
# compose.yaml
services:
  web:
    build: ./web
    ports: ["8080:80"]
  api:
    build: ./api
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    volumes: [dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
volumes:
  dbdata:

docker compose up -d && docker compose down && docker compose up -d   # the data survives
